strengths: Addresses an important problem: imputing missing protected attributes can produce misleading fairness assessments. Adversarially training the imputer is a plausible extension of existing fair-GNN methods.
Reports meaningful improvements on BAIL. With GCN, BFtS improves F1 from FairGNN's 0.86 to 0.907 and reduces equal-opportunity disparity from 4.1% to 1.7%, while also improving average precision.

Evaluation includes synthetic data, three real datasets, GCN and GAT architectures, relevant FairGNN and RNF baselines, fairness–accuracy trade-off plots, and varying attribute availability. Results are averaged over ten runs, and a code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The central worst-case interpretation is insufficiently established. Equation (8) optimizes cross-entropy and covariance surrogates without demonstrating that they identify plausible completions with maximal demographic-parity or equal-opportunity violations. Improving adversary predictability can also reflect changes in imputed group proportions. Neither analysis nor direct measurements of imputed versus ground-truth fairness establish that BFtS corrects the optimistic fairness estimation motivating the paper.

The contribution over FairGNN is not adequately isolated. BFtS changes both imputer training and the classification loss through LDAM, but there is no FairGNN-plus-LDAM control or ablation that disables only the imputer's adversarial updates. Removing fairness losses more broadly does not identify the benefit of adversarial imputation. Furthermore, Figure 4 shows mixed advantages on CREDIT and GERMAN.

The missingness experiments do not sufficiently test the motivating setting. They vary observed protected attributes from 20% to 50% of training nodes, but do not clearly specify the masking mechanism or evaluate missingness dependent on protected group, outcome, or graph structure. Robustness to systematically biased data collection therefore remains unverified.

The training specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 references Equations (2) and (4) for classifier and imputer updates, omitting the adversarial terms specified in Equations (6) and (8). Figure 2's caption says the imputer maximizes the adversarial loss, whereas Equation (8) minimizes it. These discrepancies leave the implemented optimization unclear.

Numerical reporting and reproducibility require improvement. Table 3 labels synthetic DP/EQOP values as percentages but reports 0.72/0.08, whereas Figure 3 shows approximately 72%/8%. The manuscript also leaves validation/test partitions, masking randomness, optimizer settings, hyperparameter search ranges, and the meaning of the reported uncertainty unspecified. Together, these gaps limit confidence in the empirical conclusions.
